title: Chapter 78 — The Psychology of Pricing & Value
intro: Anchors, framing, value construction, and the fairness instinct.

sections.title: How Customers Process Price
sections.content:
People do not evaluate price in absolute terms. They evaluate it relative to an anchor. The first number they hear becomes the anchor against which everything else is judged.

This is why good-better-best works. When you show a $1,800 dishwasher first, the $1,200 dishwasher feels like a deal. When you show the $600 dishwasher first, the $1,200 dishwasher feels expensive.

Present in ascending order: start with the entry option, then the mid-range recommendation, then the premium. The middle option wins most often because it feels like the reasonable choice between two extremes.

sections.title: Value Framing
sections.content:
Never let the customer evaluate the price in isolation. Always frame it against time, use, or comparison.

Time framing: 'Over the 10-year life of this dishwasher, that is about $3 a month more than the cheaper one.' Use framing: 'If you run it 5 times a week, that is 12 cents per load.' Comparison framing: 'The difference between these two is $400. For that, you get zeolite drying which means you never towel-dry a dish again.'

The goal is not to make the price disappear — it is to make the value visible.

sections.title: The Discount Trap
sections.content:
'I will take $100 off' feels small on a $2,000 appliance. But if your margin is 25 percent — $500 gross profit — that $100 discount is 20 percent of your profit. Gone.

To recover that $100 in profit, you need to sell an additional $400 at the same margin. Discounting is easy. Recovering the margin is hard.

When you must negotiate, trade — do not give. 'I can sharpen the price if we do the range and dishwasher together. The package lets me work with some flexibility.' Every concession should move toward a bigger deal, not a smaller margin.
